Are incoming Democratic senators James Talarico of Texas and Adam Hamilton of Kansas attempting to lead a major reset of American politics?

   In their victory speeches, they both called for an end to the warring, trolling, eye-gouging tactics that have taken over Washington.

   “We are tired of being pitted against each other,” Talarico said. “We are tired of being told to hate each other. It has been 10 years of this kind of politics. Politics as bloodsport…People across the spectrum are hungry for a different kind of politics.” 

   In Kansas, Hamilton had a similar message. He said he would attempt to be GOP Sen. Jerry Moran of Kansas’ “best friend.”

   “I want us to model what it looks like when thoughtful people work with each other instead of slinging mud at each other,” Hamilton said.

   Idealism among new lawmakers is as old as the Lincoln Memorial (there was even a movie made about it in 1939). Hamilton wants people to stop slinging mud, but Washington has been awfully muddy lately.

   There are a tremendous amount of new lawmakers, though, from both parties. And it’s possible that one message that resonates in Washington is an openness toward bipartisanship. President Trump has hinted at it. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D., N.Y.) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.) are suggesting they’d be open to it.

   The question I’m hearing most from readers, friends and family members is this: What are Democrats going to do? Talarico and Hamilton could be part of that conversation.

Talarico and Hamilton Called for Cooler Heads. Will They Prevail?
 
Plus, the White House battles to keep Trump’s conservative coalition together, and Democrats plan to roll back trade war with Canada
 
 
NATHAN HOWARD/REUTERS
 

Good morning. Are incoming Democratic senators James Talarico of Texas and Adam Hamilton of Kansas attempting to lead a major reset of American politics?

 

In their victory speeches, they both called for an end to the warring, trolling, eye-gouging tactics that have taken over Washington.

 

“We are tired of being pitted against each other,” Talarico said. “We are tired of being told to hate each other. It has been 10 years of this kind of politics. Politics as bloodsport…People across the spectrum are hungry for a different kind of politics.” 

 

In Kansas, Hamilton had a similar message. He said he would attempt to be GOP Sen. Jerry Moran of Kansas’ “best friend.”

 

“I want us to model what it looks like when thoughtful people work with each other instead of slinging mud at each other,” Hamilton said.

 

Idealism among new lawmakers is as old as the Lincoln Memorial (there was even a movie made about it in 1939). Hamilton wants people to stop slinging mud, but Washington has been awfully muddy lately.

 

There are a tremendous amount of new lawmakers, though, from both parties. And it’s possible that one message that resonates in Washington is an openness toward bipartisanship. President Trump has hinted at it. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D., N.Y.) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.) are suggesting they’d be open to it.

 

The question I’m hearing most from readers, friends and family members is this: What are Democrats going to do? Talarico and Hamilton could be part of that conversation.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Elizabeth Warren: The Democratic senator from Massachusetts is expected to head the Senate Banking Committee in the next Congress—and Wall Street is bracing itself.

 

Jobs: The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release October’s jobs report at 8:30 a.m. ET.

 

Trump’s Friday: The president is scheduled to hold policy meetings earlier in the day, then participate in a Diwali celebration at 1:30 p.m. He will then head to Florida where he will deliver remarks at the UP.Summit held at the Kennedy Space Center.

What I’m Following

 
 
 

The White House has told conservative groups: We’re watching you. The White House Office of Public Liaison sent a memo to more than 3,000 conservative organizations that laid out a list of Trump’s accomplishments. There were high-profile defections from the group in the hours after the election, and the administration is trying to prevent it from splintering further. “As always, we are monitoring statements, press releases, and media engagements from your organizations,” the memo said.

 

Canada tariffs are an early Democrat target. Democrats are eyeing Trump’s trade war with Canada as the first target in a campaign to roll back his administration’s tariff agenda, according to the party’s senior trade lawmaker in the Senate. Sen. Ron Wyden (D., Ore.) said he is already talking with colleagues about legislation to push against Trump’s second-term levies come January.

 

Trump has little room for maneuvering the Supreme Court. Trump put three justices on the Supreme Court during his first term. Now, voters have likely guaranteed that he won’t get a fourth, as the Democrats’ midterm blowout gave them a Senate majority that will make it easy to block Trump judicial nominees, especially for any Supreme Court vacancies that may come up in 2027 or 2028.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• A federal district judge has temporarily blocked construction of a 250-foot arch Trump plans to build near Arlington National Cemetery.

 

• Israel is suddenly confronted with a less friendly America after midterm elections brought to power more Democrats who question U.S. support for the country.

 

• Trump signed a proclamation that he said would designate the White House’s Oval Office and Cabinet Room as landmarks to prevent future presidents from making major changes to them.

 

• The MAGA faithful face the unthinkable: Is the end of their movement nigh?

 
 
 

What I’m Reading

• Florida Democrats Hold On to House Seats, but Redistricting Could Spell Future Trouble. (Orlando Sentinel)

 
 
 

This Week in Washington History

 

On this day in 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected the 16th U.S. president, becoming the first Republican to hold the office. He triumphed over three other candidates, winning 39.7% of the vote.
